title: Neural Synchrony Between Socially Interacting Language Models
one_liner: The paper measures how closely two language models change their internal activity over time during a shared task, because stronger alignment tracks better coordination.
lead: People who work together often line up in timing: they respond at the right moment, use the same context, and keep the conversation moving toward the same goal. This paper asks whether two language models show a similar kind of coordination inside their computations when they interact. The authors define neural synchrony as temporal alignment between the models' internal states during a social simulation, then test whether that alignment rises when the models coordinate well. The result matters because it gives a measurable way to study multi-model interaction below the level of surface text.

problem.h2: Surface dialogue alone does not show whether two models are truly coordinating
paras: Two language models can produce a plausible conversation even when their internal processing is poorly aligned. One model may answer late, ignore the other model's update, or shift to a different subgoal. Text alone hides that mismatch because the final sentences may still look coherent.

If we want to study social behavior in model-to-model interaction, we need a signal that changes during the exchange itself. The paper argues that internal temporal alignment can serve as that signal because a coordinated pair should update in compatible ways while they react to the same evolving context.

Without such a measure, claims about multi-model social behavior stay vague. We can count task success, but we cannot tell whether success came from real coordination or from one model doing most of the work while the other happened to stay out of the way.

callout.html: We need a direct measure of internal coordination, because fluent dialogue alone does not reveal whether two models are aligned while they interact.

steps.text: The system places language models into interaction tasks because synchrony only makes sense when the models must react to each other over time.

steps.b: Record internal states at matched turns
steps.text: For each turn, the paper extracts hidden state values from both models so that the comparison uses aligned time points from the same dialogue.
The method computes how strongly those internal states track each other across the interaction because synchronized changes indicate shared adjustment to the same conversation.
The paper also measures task quality, engagement, and timing alignment so that synchrony can be checked against observable interaction outcomes.
If high synchrony and strong performance rise together, the measure is useful because it reflects coordination that affects the task rather than random internal similarity.

paras: The paper introduces neural synchrony as a representational-level metric for interacting language models. Instead of judging multi-model social behavior only from outputs, it measures how the models' internal states align over time during the exchange.

hidden.name: Temporal alignment of internal states across interacting models
paras: The paper's key quantity is not the final answer and not the literal overlap between two messages. It is the extent to which the two models change their internal states together as the interaction unfolds. If one model shifts topic, updates its plan, or responds to new evidence, the other model should show a compatible shift when coordination is strong.

This quantity is hidden because users never see those internal state signals. The paper treats them as a trace of each model's processing state at each turn. Strong synchrony means the traces move in step over time, while weak synchrony means the models are reacting to the exchange in unrelated ways.

The authors show that this hidden quantity is informative because it tracks both social engagement and temporal alignment. That makes it useful as a proxy for coordination, since a coordinated pair should process the same evolving context in a compatible temporal pattern.

heat.caption: The darker path runs from matched turn states to synchrony to task quality, because that chain tests whether internal alignment reflects real coordination.

reads.html: Synchrony asks whether the two models are updating together while the dialogue moves forward.
The paper defines synchrony during social simulation as temporal alignment among internal representations and tests whether that alignment covaries with social performance.

paras: A multi-model interaction is a sequence of mutual updates. Each model reads the current exchange, adjusts its internal state, and produces the next response. If the pair is coordinating well, those updates should stay compatible because both models are responding to the same context and adapting to each other's behavior.

That is why synchrony can help. It does not rely on one lucky final answer. Instead, it looks at the full trajectory of internal change. A coordinated pair should repeatedly align in timing and direction, because each turn depends on the same evolving exchange. A poorly coordinated pair should drift apart, because one model will update toward a different local objective or fail to absorb the other model's last move.

The correlation with task quality matters because it shows that synchrony is not merely a static similarity score. High synchrony is useful only if it rises when the pair performs better, because that is the test that separates task-relevant coordination from accidental resemblance. The paper reports that link, which supports the claim that synchrony captures an internal feature tied to social coordination.

math.h2: A simple way to write the idea
math.words: Synchrony is the average alignment between the two models' internal state vectors over matched turns in a dialogue.
symbols: overall synchrony score for one interaction
internal state of model A at turn t
internal state of model B at turn t
a similarity function that scores how closely two states line up

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a dialogue has 4 matched turns.
At those turns, the alignment scores are 0.8, 0.7, 0.9, and 0.6.
If a second dialogue gets 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.2, its synchrony score is 0.275.
The paper then checks whether the 0.75 interaction also performs better, because a useful synchrony measure should rise with coordination quality.

math.note: The exact similarity function can vary. The core point is that the score summarizes whether the two models move together over time.

charts.title: Weak coordination case
charts.note: Low internal alignment tends to come with weaker interaction quality because the two models are not adjusting in step.

charts.title: Strong coordination case
charts.note: The paper reports that stronger synchrony tracks stronger social performance because the pair processes the shared context more coherently.

items.b: Synchrony may rise for the wrong reason.
items.html: Two models built from the same base system may look aligned even when the interaction is shallow, so the metric needs controls because shared architecture can create similarity without genuine coordination.
If the measurement compares states from mismatched points in the dialogue, the synchrony score becomes unreliable because the timing signal is broken.
A strong correlation shows that synchrony is informative, but it does not prove that synchrony causes better coordination because both could be driven by another factor such as model quality.

items.b: Done right: synchrony becomes a useful probe.
items.html: When timing is aligned and architecture effects are controlled, the metric helps because it reveals coordination patterns that do not appear in text alone.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small two-model interaction benchmark with negotiation, collaborative planning, or question answering. For each dialogue, log hidden states from both models at each turn, compute a synchrony score, and also score the joint outcome. Then compare high-synchrony dialogues with low-synchrony dialogues. The demo should show that stronger synchrony usually comes with better timing and stronger joint outcomes, because that would confirm that the metric is tracking real coordination.
demo.closing: The demo should make clear that synchrony matters only if it predicts better coordination, because a coordination metric is useful only when it tracks better joint task quality.
